<reason>PRO built a coherent causal story (temporary, lumpy revenue; Dutch disease; smoothing; distributions can sit downstream of a fund but not vice versa) and then progressively narrowed the debate onto the bust year. Its pressure question forcing CON to choose between zero payments, borrowing, or boom-year savings (a fund by another name) was the decisive move, and CON's honest answer—"potentially to zero"—handed PRO its closing. PRO also turned CON's Alaska guardianship point into support for funds and gave a plausible risk-pooling argument ("asking every household to run its own sovereign wealth fund, alone"). CON argued with discipline and had one genuinely strong live point—household borrowing costs exceeding fund returns, so debt repaid in the boom keeps paying off in the bust—and correctly noted PRO assumes a "sufficient" payout. But CON never fully neutralized the inflation/absorption problem (conceding foreign retention reduces demand), largely accepted that the smoothed child is better protected, and left PRO's core framing intact. PRO's clipped rebuttal is a minor execution cost that does not change the outcome.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's Q1 trilemma [B3.1] and its follow-through in [B4.6]/[B5.1]-[B5.3]: forcing CON to admit dividends fall "potentially to zero" in a multi-year bust, then framing CON's fallback (households saving and repaying wisely) as requiring every poor family to self-insure without diversification—directly damaging CON's durability claim.</best_rebuttal>
